title: Virtual reality and augmented reality-supported K-12 STEM learning: trends, advantages and challenges
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) in K-12 STEM education and the need for a broad synthesis of how these technologies are being used, for whom, and with what reported benefits and challenges. The authors note that prior reviews tended to focus on earlier studies, on a single discipline, or on narrower technology subsets, leaving an updated and wider view of VR/AR-supported K-12 STEM learning incomplete.

To answer this gap, the study systematically reviewed 117 empirical articles published from 2010 to 2022, using PRISMA procedures and a technology-based learning model. The review coded learning subject, device type, participant age group, research method, sample size, and learning strategy, with an emphasis on K-12 STEM contexts. The included studies covered elementary, middle, and high school students, with the largest share in elementary school; mathematics was the second most common subject after science, and there were far fewer studies in technology or engineering.

The review found that VR/AR was most often associated with positive effects on academic achievement, motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, attention, and some higher-order cognitive skills. It also supported learning processes such as engagement, visualization, inquiry, collaborative learning, and interaction. At the same time, the paper identified recurring implementation challenges, including distraction, operational difficulties, teacher classroom-management and design burdens, and school-level constraints such as cost, infrastructure, and privacy concerns. Overall, the paper concludes that VR/AR is promising for K-12 STEM learning but needs better-designed implementations, more attention to immersive tools, and more research in underexplored areas such as technology, engineering, and senior high school settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using PRISMA and explicit coding procedures, but it is not a primary causal study and does not estimate pooled effects. The evidence is therefore syntheses-level and descriptive, with moderate credibility for mapping trends but limited for causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports several positive educational associations, including a large attention effect in one included study (d=1.28) and recurring improvements in achievement, motivation, and engagement. At the same time, it emphasizes mixed implementation realities and substantial school/teacher constraints, so the overall impact is promising but not uniformly strong.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of VR/AR-supported K-12 STEM learning, including immersive and non-immersive simulations, virtual labs, and game-based learning activities used to teach science and mathematics concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes mathematics among the STEM domains studied (22 of 117 articles) and reports that VR/AR was often associated with improved understanding and achievement in STEM learning, but the mathematics-specific evidence base was comparatively smaller than science. The paper synthesizes prior empirical studies rather than estimating a single pooled effect, so no overall meta-analytic effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes across included empirical studies (e.g., achievement tests, understanding, learning gains)
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; 22 studies in mathematics

finding.finding_summary: Across the 117-study review, science was the dominant domain (77 studies), and the authors conclude that VR/AR generally had a positive impact on learners, especially by helping them understand abstract scientific concepts and conduct virtual inquiry/experimentation. The review reports multiple included studies showing higher achievement and better conceptual understanding, but because this is a systematic review, it does not provide one pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Science achievement, conceptual understanding, inquiry/experiment outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review found repeated positive effects on motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, satisfaction, attention, and engagement. For example, it cites one study where AR-based science learning improved attention with a large effect size of d=1.28, and numerous studies reported gains in learning motivation and self-efficacy.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-efficacy, attitudes, satisfaction, attention, engagement, cognitive load
finding.study_size: n=117 studies reviewed; many sub-findings across included studies
finding.effect_size: d=1.28 reported for attention in one included study; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that VR/AR can support higher-order skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, analytical ability, metacognitive awareness, and collaboration. However, these outcomes were less frequently studied than achievement or motivation, and the paper synthesizes heterogeneous primary studies rather than estimating a pooled effect.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, metacognitive awareness, collaboration/cooperative ability

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests VR/AR can improve learning efficiency and effectiveness in some cases, but it also documents implementation burdens such as device-operation problems, classroom management challenges, setup time, and technical competence demands. Only one included study explicitly reported improved learning efficiency, while several others described inefficiencies or mixed results.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency/effectiveness; implementation and classroom process observations

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the review identifies substantial implementation barriers: high equipment cost, inadequate infrastructure, lack of private virtual space, privacy concerns, and teacher classroom-management burdens. These are framed as recurring school-level challenges rather than quantified effects, indicating mixed system-level impact despite pedagogical promise.
finding.measure: School-level implementation constraints, cost, infrastructure, privacy, and classroom management
